pages.html:

Tides

A tide is the slow rise and fall of the sea, twice a day on most coasts. It is caused mostly by the pull of the Moon on the water of the Earth.

When the Sun and the Moon pull along the same line the tides are larger; these are called spring tides. People who lived by the sea planned fishing, travel and harvests of shellfish around the tide tables.

pages.title: Lighthouses
pages.html:
Home | About | Log in

Lighthouses

A lighthouse is a tower with a bright lamp at the top, built on a coast or a rock to warn ships away from danger and guide them home at night.

Each lighthouse flashed in its own pattern so sailors could tell which one they saw. For centuries keepers lived in them and climbed the stairs every evening to light the lamp.

pages.title: Bread
pages.html:
Home | About | Log in

Bread

Bread is made from flour and water, usually with yeast that makes the dough rise before it is baked. It is one of the oldest prepared foods people made.

Nearly every culture had its own bread: flat, round, braided, sour or sweet. Sharing bread was a sign of welcome, and the word companion once meant someone you share bread with.

pages.title: Lullabies
pages.html:
Home | About | Log in

Lullabies

A lullaby is a quiet song sung to help a child fall asleep. The melodies are simple and slow, and often rock back and forth like a cradle.

Lullabies were passed from parents to children by ear for many generations, so the same tune could have many different words in different villages.

pages.title: Seed banks
pages.html:
Home | About | Log in

Seed banks

A seed bank stores seeds of many kinds of plants so that they are not lost. The seeds are dried and kept cold, and some stay alive for hundreds of years.

The largest vault was built inside a frozen mountain in the far north. Its keepers said it was a promise to people not yet born that the gardens could be planted again.

pages.title: Kites
pages.html:
Home | About | Log in

Kites

A kite is a light frame covered with paper or cloth that flies on the wind at the end of a long string. Kites were flown for play, for festivals and to measure the weather.

Children learned that a kite needs a tail to stay steady and that it climbs best when you walk backwards into the wind.

pages.title: Bells
pages.html:
Home | About | Log in

Bells

A bell is a hollow cup of metal that rings when it is struck. Towns hung large bells in towers to mark the hours, call people together and warn of fire or storm.

A set of tuned bells is called a carillon. Casting a large bell took weeks, and its note could not be known for certain until it had cooled and was struck for the first time.

pages.title: Maps
pages.html:
Home | About | Log in

Maps

A map is a drawing of a place seen from above, made smaller so that it can be carried. Maps show coasts, rivers, roads and names so a traveller can find the way.

Old map makers drew what they knew and left the rest empty or filled it with guesses. A map says as much about the people who drew it as about the land.

pages.title: Weaving
pages.html:
Home | About | Log in

Weaving

Weaving makes cloth by crossing two sets of threads on a loom: the warp runs lengthwise and the weft is passed over and under it.

Patterns were remembered as counts and songs. Some weavers put one small mistake into every cloth on purpose, to say that only made things are perfect, not makers.

pages.title: Tea
pages.html:
Home | About | Log in

Tea

Tea is a drink made by pouring hot water over the dried leaves of the tea plant. After water, it was the most widely drunk drink in the world.

In many places making tea for a guest was a small ceremony: warming the pot, waiting, pouring. The waiting was considered part of the drink.

pages.title: Choirs
pages.html:
Home | About | Log in

Choirs

A choir is a group of people who sing together, usually in several parts at once: high and low voices that fit into chords.

Singers in a choir listen as much as they sing. People often said that singing together made a room of strangers feel like one creature breathing.

pages.title: Clocks
pages.html:
Home | About | Log in

Clocks

A clock measures and shows the time. The first mechanical clocks used falling weights and gears, and had no faces: they only rang a bell each hour.

Later a swinging pendulum made clocks accurate enough to keep minutes. Towns set their clocks by the Sun, so every town had a slightly different noon until railways needed one shared time.

pages.title: Bridges
pages.html:
Home | About | Log in

Bridges

A bridge carries a path over a river, a valley or a road. The arch was the great old idea: stones leaning on each other so that the weight pushes sideways into the banks.

Many bridges had a small shrine or a lamp in the middle. People met there, traded there, and said goodbye there.

pages.title: Gardens

Gardens

A garden is a piece of ground where plants are grown on purpose, for food, for medicine or simply because they are beautiful.

Gardeners planted trees whose shade they would never sit in. A garden is one of the few things people made that was never finished.
